candidates.exact_span: The facility discharge point into the San Juan River is in State of New Mexico waters approximately two miles upstream of the Navajo Nation's boundary. Since 40 CFR §122.4(d) requires NPDES permits also be protective of a downstream state or tribe's water quality standards, the water quality standards of the Navajo Nation have been considered.
candidates.computation_change_reason: Whether limits are derived from New Mexico standards alone or must also satisfy Navajo Nation downstream-protection requirements can change which numeric WQBELs are treated as enforceable at the discharge point.

candidates.exact_span: Where these technology-based permit limits do not protect water quality or the designated uses, additional water quality-based effluent limitations and/or conditions are included in the NPDES permits.
candidates.computation_change_reason: Interpretation of when technology-based limits are insufficient triggers inclusion of WQBELs versus reliance on TBLs alone, changing which enforceable numeric limit applies for compliance comparison.

candidates.exact_span: State narrative and numerical water quality standards are used in conjunction with EPA criteria and other available toxicity information to determine the adequacy of technology-based permit limits and the need for additional water quality-based controls.
candidates.computation_change_reason: Different readings of which source documents (state narrative vs numerical standards vs EPA criteria vs toxicity data) govern adequacy can change the derived numeric limits selected for evaluation.

candidates.exact_span: The general and specific stream standards are provided in New Mexico State Standards for Interstate and Intrastate Surface Water (20.6.4 NMAC, effective September 12, 2018). The facility discharges into the San Juan River in segment number 20.6.4.401 of the San Juan Basin.
candidates.computation_change_reason: The cited NMAC version and receiving-water segment identify which state numerical criteria apply; a different segment or effective standard set would yield different applicable numeric limits.

candidates.exact_span: The designated uses of the receiving waters are public and industrial water supply, irrigation, livestock watering, wildlife habitat, primary contact, marginal coldwater aquatic life and warmwater aquatic life.
candidates.computation_change_reason: Designated uses determine which water-quality criteria and narrative standards are invoked for limit derivation (A) and can determine which parameters or use-specific monitoring conditions are in scope for obligation evaluation (B).

candidates.exact_span: The Navajo Nation WQS and New Mexico WQS are very similar and protection to NMWQS at the point of discharge would also be protective of downstream Navajo Nation waters, except for some of the parameters as discussed below.
candidates.computation_change_reason: The exception for unspecified parameters means some limits may follow Navajo Nation rather than New Mexico standards (A). For measurements without numeric results, whether a parameter falls under the exception affects whether a missing result is evaluated against an unresolved alternate limit or classified under a different missing-evidence state (C).

candidates.exact_span: The Navajo Nation designated uses of the San Juan River at the point it enters the Navajo Nation are domestic water supply, primary human contact, secondary human contact, agricultural water supply, fish consumption, aquatic & wildlife habitat and livestock watering.
candidates.computation_change_reason: If Navajo Nation standards govern for excepted parameters, these downstream designated uses (which differ from New Mexico uses at discharge) can change applicable criteria and associated monitoring scope.
